explain.say: A scout ant finds food and heads home, dabbing the tip of its abdomen on the ground to leave a trail of chemical scent called a pheromone.

explain.say: Nestmates follow the trail by sweeping their two antennae, which smell the pheromone. Each ant that finds food adds more scent on the way back, so the trail grows stronger and attracts even more ants.

explain.say: Ants on a shorter route return sooner and lay scent more often, so the shortest path ends up with the strongest trail. This is how a line of ants seems to find the best route.

faq.a: A pheromone is a chemical message that animals of the same species smell. An ant lays a trail by touching its abdomen to the ground, leaving a line of scent other ants can follow.
asks: How do ants mark a path?

faq.q: Why do ants walk in a line?
faq.a: Every ant follows the same scent trail with its antennae and adds more scent if it finds food. The trail gets stronger the more ants use it, which keeps them in a neat line.
asks: How do ants use their antennae?
Why do more and more ants come?

faq.q: How do ants find the shortest path?
faq.a: Ants on a shorter path make round trips faster, so they lay scent more often. That path builds up the strongest smell, and soon most ants use it. No single ant plans the route.
asks: Are ants clever at finding routes?
How do ants choose a route?

faq.q: Why does an ant trail disappear?
faq.a: Pheromones evaporate within minutes to hours. When food runs out, returning ants stop laying scent, the trail fades, and ants stop coming, so the colony does not waste trips.
asks: How do ants know food has run out?

faq.q: How do I stop ants following a trail into my kitchen?
faq.a: Wiping the trail with soapy water or vinegar removes the pheromone, so new ants lose the way. Sealing gaps and cleaning up crumbs stops them finding food in the first place.
asks: How do you break an ant trail?
Why do ants come back to the same spot?

facts: Foraging ants lay pheromone trails that other ants follow and reinforce, a form of positive feedback.
In experiments with two bridges to food, Argentine ant colonies came to use the shorter bridge.
